definition: In this historical psychology usage, protensity means time as it is immediately lived as a continuous stretch or duration in experience. The passage contrasts this direct felt continuity with intensity, suggesting that some writers treated our earliest time-sense as a continuous experiential flow.

provenance.scope: Source record fca72454f1995c69b072; pinned source text

reasons: The packet supports protensity as a term for time perceived as continuous duration or 'continuous protensity,' but it does not support the added claim that this was 'our earliest time-sense.'

The statement that 'some writers treated our earliest time-sense as a continuous experiential flow' goes beyond the passage; the source discusses one writer’s view about duration being perceived as intensity rather than time, not a broader historical consensus or earliest-stage theory.

The definition claims that “protensity means time as it is immediately lived as a continuous stretch or duration in experience.” The packet only states that, in the first instance, time is “not… perceived as time—i.e. as continuous ‘protensity,’ but as intensity,” and does not explicitly define protensity as an “immediately lived” continuous duration.

The definition says it “suggests that some writers treated our earliest time-sense as a continuous experiential flow.” The packet mentions “the first instance” and attributes the contrast to Ward (and references Hamilton’s term), but it does not support the specific framing “our earliest time-sense” or “continuous experiential flow.”
